subtopicTitle: Harmonics and overtones — on strings and in pipes

cards.front: Define the fundamental frequency of a vibrating string or air column.
cards.back: The lowest possible frequency of a standing wave satisfying the boundary conditions, corresponding to the simplest mode with maximum wavelength.

cards.front: What is the precise distinction between a harmonic and an overtone?
cards.back: A harmonic is any integer multiple of the fundamental frequency (1st harmonic = fundamental). An overtone is any frequency above the fundamental; the nth overtone is the (n+1)th harmonic.

cards.front: State the frequencies of the first three harmonics on a string fixed at both ends (length L, wave speed v).
State the frequencies of the first three harmonics for a pipe closed at one end (length L, wave speed v).
State the frequencies of the first three harmonics for a pipe open at both ends (length L, wave speed v).
cards.back: $f_n = n v/(2L)$ for n = 1,2,3,… (all integer harmonics)

cards.front: Derive why a closed pipe supports only odd harmonics using boundary conditions.
cards.back: Closed end requires displacement node; open end requires antinode. Standing-wave condition: L = (2n-1)λ/4, n=1,2,3,… Thus frequencies are odd multiples of v/(4L).

cards.front: Why does a string fixed at both ends produce all integer harmonics while a closed pipe does not?
cards.back: String boundaries are symmetric (node-node), allowing λ_n = 2L/n. Closed pipe has asymmetric boundaries (node-antinode), restricting solutions to odd multiples only.

cards.front: In musical terms, which harmonic corresponds to the first overtone on a guitar string vs. a clarinet (closed pipe)?
cards.back: Guitar (string): 2nd harmonic. Clarinet (closed): 3rd harmonic (first available overtone after fundamental).
